passages.heading: Lagrange point
passages.text:
In celestial mechanics, the **Lagrange points** (/ləˈɡrɑːndʒ/), also called the **Lagrangian points** or **libration points**, are points of equilibrium for small-mass objects under the gravitational influence of two massive orbiting bodies. Mathematically, this involves the solution of the restricted three-body problem.<sup>[1]</sup>

Normally, the two massive bodies exert an unbalanced gravitational force at a point, altering the orbit of any other celestial body at that point. At the Lagrange points, the gravitational forces of the two large bodies and the centrifugal pseudo-force balance each other.<sup>[2]</sup> This can make Lagrange points an excellent location for satellites, as orbit corrections, and hence fuel requirements, needed to maintain the desired orbit are kept at a minimum.

passages.heading: Lagrange point
passages.text: The European Space Agency's earlier Gaia telescope, and its newly launched Euclid, also occupy orbits around L<sub>2</sub>. Gaia keeps a tighter Lissajous orbit around L<sub>2</sub>, while Euclid follows a halo orbit similar to JWST. Each of the space observatories benefits from being far enough from Earth's shadow to utilize solar panels for power, from not needing much power or propellant for station-keeping, from not being subjected to the Earth's magnetospheric effects, and from having direct line-of-sight to Earth for data transfer.

passages.heading: *Gaia* (spacecraft)
passages.text: To study the precise position and motion of its target objects, the spacecraft monitored each of them about 70 times<sup>[11]</sup> over the five years of the nominal mission (2014–2019), and about as many during its extension.<sup>[12]</sup><sup>[13]</sup> Due to its detectors degrading more slowly than initially expected, the data acquisition phase of the mission was given an extension,<sup>[14]</sup> lasting until March 27, 2025, when scientists at the ESA switched off *Gaia* after more than a decade of service.<sup>[15]</sup> *Gaia* targeted objects brighter than magnitude 20 in a broad photometric band that covered the extended visual range between near-UV and near infrared;<sup>[16]</sup> such objects represent approximately 1% of the Milky Way population.<sup>[11]</sup> Additionally, *Gaia* was expected to detect thousands to tens of thousands of Jupiter-sized exoplanets beyond the Solar System using astrometry,<sup>[17]</sup><sup>[18]</sup><sup>[19]</sup><sup>[20]</sup> 500,000 quasars outside this galaxy and tens of thousands of known and new asteroids and comets within the Solar System.<sup>[21]</sup><sup>[22]</sup><sup>[23]</sup>

passages.heading: *Gaia* (spacecraft)
passages.text: The successor to the *Hipparcos* mission (1989–1993), *Gaia* is part of ESA's Horizon 2000+ long-term scientific program. *Gaia* was launched on 19 December 2013 by Arianespace using a Soyuz ST-B/Fregat-MT rocket flying from Kourou in French Guiana.<sup>[24]</sup><sup>[25]</sup> The spacecraft operated in a Lissajous orbit around the Sun–Earth L<sub>2</sub> Lagrangian point. The science observation officially ended on 15 January 2025.<sup>[26]</sup>

passages.heading: MISSION / A JOURNEY TO THE DARK UNIVERSE
passages.text:
ESA’s Euclid mission is designed to map the large-scale structure of the Universe and help understand its two biggest mysteries: dark matter and dark energy.

Only 5% of the Universe is made up of visible matter.

passages.heading: Milestone / (Clicca sui pallini a sinistra per far scorrere il testo) / ROADMAP
passages.text:
Do you see that ship? On board is Euclid, the ESA satellite that will investigate the dark side of the Universe. It departed on April 17, 2023, from the port of Savona bound for Cape Canaveral, where its launch into space awaits it in July.

Testing simulations for Euclid have begun at ESA's Mission Control Center.

Immediately following launch, the satellite and its scientific instruments will undergo a series of tests for approximately 30 days to ensure everything is functioning correctly.

During this 30-day period, Euclid will reach L2: a point 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, from which it will observe the deep universe for six years.

ESA's Mission Control Center will take charge of Euclid just seconds after launch and will be responsible for its operation and monitoring its health throughout its operational life.

passages.heading: Milestone / (Clicca sui pallini a sinistra per far scorrere il testo) / ROADMAP
passages.text:
The exciting countdown, a tradition that accompanies the start of space missions, will commence from the main control room.

On June 27, 2023, ESA's Euclid space telescope was encapsulated within a SpaceX Falcon 9 fairing, which will keep Euclid safe and clean during the final days before liftoff and protect the spacecraft from Earth's atmosphere during launch.

Euclid Takes Flight! Excitement Grips the Consortium!

Euclid has finally embarked on its journey! The excitement across the entire Consortium is palpable!

On July 1, 2023, Euclid soared into space atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Within four weeks, the satellite traversed 1.5 million kilometers, reaching its designated location at the Lagrange L2 point.

In celestial mechanics, the **Lagrange points** (/ləˈɡrɑːndʒ/), also called the **Lagrangian points** or **libration points**, are points of equilibrium for small-mass objects under the gravitational influence of two massive orbiting bodies. Mathematically, this involves the solution of the restricted three-body problem.<sup>[1]</sup>

Normally, the two massive bodies exert an unbalanced gravitational force at a point, altering the orbit of any other celestial body at that point. At the Lagrange points, the gravitational forces of the two large bodies and the centrifugal pseudo-force balance each other.<sup>[2]</sup> This can make Lagrange points an excellent location for satellites, as orbit corrections, and hence fuel requirements, needed to maintain the desired orbit are kept at a minimum. 

Section: Lagrange point
The European Space Agency's earlier Gaia telescope, and its newly launched Euclid, also occupy orbits around L<sub>2</sub>. Gaia keeps a tighter Lissajous orbit around L<sub>2</sub>, while Euclid follows a halo orbit similar to JWST. Each of the space observatories benefits from being far enough from Earth's shadow to utilize solar panels for power, from not needing much power or propellant for station-keeping, from not being subjected to the Earth's magnetospheric effects, and from having direct line-of-sight to Earth for data transfer.
